newsitem.title: INDIA: Foreign firms shaken by India insurance move.
newsitem.headline: Foreign firms shaken by India insurance move.

text.p: International insurers voiced disappointment on Wednesday over the government's decision to withdraw a bill that would have allowed foreign companies into the lucrative sector.

"We are extremely disappointed. Everybody in the international community has been very patient waiting for this to happen," George Otto, chief representative at the India liaison office of Allianz AG Holdings, told Reuters.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral withdrew the insurance regulatory bill from the lower house of parliament after his coalition failed to muster enough votes to defeat an opposition-backed amendment barring the entry of foreign firms.
"We have all been building up to this. And then all of a sudden at 99-and-a-half, there goes the rug again," Otto said.
"The whole issue goes much wider than just insurance which is only one part of it, and we wonder whether this sends a signal on overall liberalisation."

The bill would have created an insurance regulatory authority to oversee the state-controlled industry, and was considered an important step towards the eventual opening up of the sector to private firms, both Indian and foreign.
Prudential Insurance Co of America senior vice president Armand Pacher said: "Anybody looking at the defeat of the bill would be disappointed unless you can see some silver lining to it."
He said Prudential had looked at India and Brazil at the same time last year, and was on its way to establishing a joint venture and starting operations in India.
"We remain very hopeful we will have an opportunity to create a fundamental improvement in the variety and products available to the Indian people," Pacher said.

Royal and Sun Alliance Insurance Group Plc's India CEO Duncan West said: "We are disappointed, but are trying to find a background to this decision. Our disappointment stems from the fact that we are very eager to enter the market."
West said Royal and Sun Alliance had polled consumers in several parts of India, and they had said "give us a choice."
"This won't change our outlook, as we have waited four years to get to this stage, and this seems to be a temporary delay. But we definitely need to know whether the bill will go through," he said.
